strengths: WildFeedback offers a useful resource contribution: 20,281 preference pairs grounded in naturally occurring feedback from real, multi-turn conversations. The pipeline addresses a relevant problem in conversational NLP and preference learning.

Experiments cover three model families, regenerated UltraFeedback baselines, and three established benchmarks. Substantial improvements over the original instruction-tuned models support the dataset’s practical utility. For example, Phi-3’s AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate increases from 24.3% to 34.9%, and its Arena-Hard score increases from 15.4% to 32.4%.

The authors validate feedback classification on 50 conversations and checklist evaluation on 200 conversations using multiple human annotators. Reporting human–human agreement provides useful context for interpreting the automated judgments.

The manuscript clearly describes the main pipeline, provides extensive prompts, identifies model checkpoints, reports major training hyperparameters, and links the dataset. The stated separation of training and evaluation users and conversations is a valuable precaution. These elements support a contribution suitable for Findings.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the benefit of actual user feedback. WildFeedback and UltraFeedback differ in prompt distribution, conversational context, response construction, and filtering. A comparison using identical WildChat prompts with genuine, omitted, or shuffled feedback would distinguish feedback learning from domain adaptation and synthetic response improvement. An SFT-only comparison would also clarify the contribution of preference optimization.

The claim that checklist evaluation more accurately reflects real-user preferences is insufficiently validated. GPT-4 extracts preferences, generates expert responses, filters on-policy pairs, and judges outputs using those extracted preferences. Figure 2 therefore measures agreement with the construction criteria, rather than independently establishing their fidelity to users. The human study reports agreement of 57.14% and κ=0.372, but provides no corresponding evaluation without checklists and no direct validation of preference-summary accuracy.

The evaluation supports a narrower population than the broad alignment claims suggest. The 540-item test set deliberately selects central preferences from prompt clusters; this does not establish that those preferences represent a majority of users. Feedback detection further restricts coverage: DSAT recall is 48.4% on the annotation sample. The acknowledged selection bias should more clearly constrain claims about diverse users, evolving preferences, and reduced bias.

Claims of significant and consistent superiority are stronger than the reported evidence. No confidence intervals or variation across training seeds are provided, despite several small differences. Table 3 also contains counterexamples: Qwen-2 trained on WF GPT-4 scores below UF GPT-4 on AlpacaEval LC (39.4 versus 40.6) and MT-Bench (7.60 versus 7.66).

Some consequential reproduction details remain unspecified, including the embedding model and precise clustering, deduplication, and user-grouping procedures for test construction; response-generation decoding settings; and sequence truncation. Appendix A.2 documents preference extraction rather than the complete response-generation template. These gaps particularly affect reconstruction of the custom evaluation.
